questions.enonce_markdown:
The personality of Jesus contributed a lot to the controversies faced during his trial.

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** In the Fourth Gospel, the trial of Jesus (18:12-19:16) is a series of confrontations before Annas and Caiaphas and then before Pilate. The controversies are caused partly by the way Jesus presents himself and behaves, and partly by the fears and interests of his opponents. The statement is largely true, though other factors also played a part.

**1. His claims about himself.** The accusations rest on claims that Jesus had made earlier: that God was his own Father, making himself equal to God (5:18), that "before Abraham was, I am" (8:58) and that "the Father and I are one" (10:30-33). At the trial, the Jewish leaders tell Pilate, "He has claimed to be the Son of God" (19:7). His strong awareness of his identity is the root of the charge of blasphemy.

**2. His confidence and dignity.** Before Annas Jesus answers the question about his teaching by saying that he has spoken openly and that those who heard him should be asked (18:20-21). When an official strikes him, he calmly asks for evidence of wrong (18:22-23). His calm refusal to be intimidated made the proceedings look unjust.

**3. His kingship.** Before Pilate the question is whether he is a king (18:33-37). Jesus answers that his kingdom "is not of this world", that he came to bear witness to the truth, and that everyone who belongs to the truth listens to his voice. This is not a political claim, yet it alarms the authorities and leaves Pilate uncertain. Pilate asks, "What is truth?" and finds no case against him (18:38).

**4. His authority.** When Pilate says he has power to release or crucify him, Jesus replies that Pilate would have no power over him unless it had been given from above (19:10-11). Even as a prisoner, Jesus speaks as one in control, so that the trial seems at times to place Pilate himself on trial.

**5. The pressure on Pilate.** The leaders turn the religious charge into a political one: "If you release him, you are no friend of the emperor" (19:12). They declare "We have no king but the emperor" (19:15). Here the personality and claims of Jesus force a choice between loyalty to him and to Caesar.

**6. Other factors.** The controversies also came from the fear of the leaders about their position and about Roman reaction, from Pilate's weakness and desire to keep order, and from the crowd's pressure. John's theological purpose also shapes his account: Jesus goes to the cross freely, as the one who lays down his life (10:17-18).

**Conclusion.** The personality of Jesus, his sense of identity, his dignity and his claims to kingship and to divine sonship, were central to the controversies of his trial. They were not the only cause, since political fears and Pilate's weakness also mattered, but without them the conflict would not have taken the form it did.
